subject: physics
question_text: A brass wire of diameter 1 mm is stretched by a load of 20 N. If the original length of the wire is 2 m and the increase in length is 0.51 mm, find (i) the stress produced in the wire, (ii) the strain, and (iii) the Young's modulus of the material of the wire.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 9 Short Answer Question 4 (printed p.100). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: d = 1 mm gives r = 0.5 × 10⁻³ m and A = πr² = 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m²; (i) stress = F/A = 20/(7.85×10⁻⁷) = 2.55 × 10⁷ N/m²; (ii) strain = ΔL/L = (0.51×10⁻³)/2 = 2.55 × 10⁻⁴; (iii) Y = stress/strain = (2.55×10⁷)/(2.55×10⁻⁴) = 1.0 × 10¹¹ N/m². All three values match the brief's independently checked arithmetic.

steps.label: Given data and the area
lines: Length L = 2 m, load F = 20 N,
steps.margin_note: Convert the diameter to a radius before squaring — that is where marks are usually lost.
steps.why: Both the stress and the Young's modulus parts need the cross-sectional area, so it has to be worked out from the given diameter before either part can be answered.
common_mistakes: Squaring the diameter instead of the radius. A = πr², and r is half the diameter.
Leaving ΔL in millimetres instead of converting it to metres.
steps.memory_tip: Halve the diameter first, then square it: r = d/2, A = πr².

steps.label: Part (i) — the stress
steps.margin_note: Divide the load by the area found above; do not recompute the area here.
steps.why: Stress is the restoring force per unit area, and since the wire is in equilibrium, this equals the applied force divided by the cross-sectional area.
common_mistakes: Using the diameter or the length in place of the area in the formula.
Losing track of the power of ten while dividing — work the exponent separately from the digits.
steps.memory_tip: σ = F/A: twenty newtons over a tiny area gives a value near 10⁷ N/m².

steps.label: Part (ii) — the strain
steps.margin_note: Keep ΔL and L in the same unit, metres, before dividing.
steps.why: Strain is a ratio of two lengths, so it must come out as a pure number; keeping ΔL and L both in metres is what makes that ratio correct.
common_mistakes: Dividing by the extension instead of the original length.
Mixing units, ΔL in mm and L in m, which shifts the power of ten.
steps.memory_tip: Strain = ΔL/L: a fraction-of-a-millimetre stretch over a two-metre wire gives strain of order 10⁻⁴.

steps.label: Part (iii) — Young's modulus
steps.margin_note: Reuse the stress and strain values found above rather than starting over from F and ΔL.
steps.why: Young's modulus is defined as stress divided by strain, so once both are known from the earlier parts, this step is a single division with no new physics.
common_mistakes: Inverting the ratio and writing Y = strain / stress.
Recomputing from F and ΔL directly instead of dividing the two earlier answers.
steps.memory_tip: Y = stress/strain: divide the two answers from parts (i) and (ii).

insider_note: This is a straight substitution question — the area from the given diameter carries the first mark, and each part (i), (ii), (iii) is a value mark on its own, so a right method with a wrong final digit still loses that step.
